title: Arjuna answers the cry at the gate
hook: Arjuna breaks a vow to answer a man at the gate, and a ruler's duty gets its name.
carry: a ruler's joy lives in the people's joy
tomorrow: a king with every pleasure, and a brother who warned him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vinaya: even a king stays a student, rooted in the elders. Today, a cry at the palace gate, and the duty it calls up.

In the Mahabharata, the five Pandava brothers share one rule: whoever walks in on a brother alone with Draupadi goes into exile. One day a brahmin runs to the palace, shouting. Thieves have driven off his cows, and nobody is protecting him. Arjuna's weapons are in that very room. Wait, and the thieves get away. Go in, and he breaks the rule. Arjuna reasons it out: if a cry at the king's gate goes unanswered, the fault falls on the king. So he walks in, takes his bow, rides after the thieves, and brings the cows back. His brother tries to excuse him. Arjuna keeps his word anyway, and leaves for twelve years of exile.
screen: `A CRY AT THE GATE.` → `THE BOW IS IN THE ROOM.` → `ANSWER IT, AND PAY THE PRICE.`

segments.voice: That story is raja dharma, the ruler's duty, in action: protecting the people is the first work of power, even when it costs. The Arthashastra writes the same duty into its chapter on the king's day. A ruler must not keep a petitioner waiting at the door, it says. When he makes himself hard to reach, business gets tangled and the people turn against him. So he hears cases himself, and promptly. It even names whose matters come first, among them children, the old, the sick and the helpless. An urgent case heard late, it warns, can become hard or impossible to set right. Then a verse still quoted in India when people talk about public service. In the happiness of his subjects lies the king's happiness. In their welfare, his welfare. What pleases the king himself, he should not count as good. What pleases his people, that is good. Here's the Hindu teaching underneath. Power isn't a prize in this tradition. It's a dharma, a duty with people attached. Arjuna answered the cry at the cost of twelve years. The Arthashastra asks less of a king, only an open gate, but it moves his happiness out of the palace and into the line outside.
screen: `RAJA DHARMA: POWER IS A DUTY.` · `DON'T KEEP PEOPLE AT THE DOOR.` · `THE HELPLESS FIRST. LATE CAN BE TOO LATE.` · `WHAT PLEASES HIS PEOPLE IS GOOD.` · then, large: `THEIR HAPPINESS IS HIS.`

segments.voice: On paper or in a note, write the name of one person who's waiting at your gate: for a reply, a visit, a little attention. If you pray, say over the name a prayer many Hindus know, sarve bhavantu sukhinah, may all be happy. If you don't, simply wish them well. Then breathe slowly, and let their good matter to you as much as your own.
The Arthashastra's opening: a king who doesn't keep people at the gate, and finds his happiness in theirs.
Your line: a ruler's joy lives in the people's joy. Arjuna answered the cry at the gate. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus call a ruler's duty raja dharma. The Arthashastra's verse on the subjects' happiness is quoted in India in talk of public service, and Arjuna's exile for the brahmin's cows is told as a lesson in that duty.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Arjuna enters Yudhishthira and Draupadi's room for his weapons to recover a brahmin's stolen cattle, then goes into twelve years' exile to keep the brothers' rule)
